name: Semaglutide
lead: Semaglutide is a peptide medication that mimics the gut hormone glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) and acts as a GLP-1 receptor agonist. Developed by Novo Nordisk, it is sold as Ozempic and Rybelsus for type 2 diabetes and as Wegovy for chronic weight management, and is given as a weekly injection or, in the case of the oral products, as a daily tablet [1][16]. It was approved in the United States in December 2017 and in Canada, the European Union and Japan in 2018 [1].

People use semaglutide to lose body fat. By dampening appetite and increasing the feeling of fullness, it lowers calorie intake, and lower body fat generally shows up as a leaner waist, a more defined jawline and sharper facial contours. In clinical trials of adults with overweight or obesity and no diabetes, the 2.4 mg weekly dose produced average weight reductions of roughly 12 to 15 percent of body weight over 68 weeks, compared with small losses on placebo [1][4][5][14]. Large outcome trials have also reported lower rates of major cardiovascular events in people with diabetes and in people with obesity and established cardiovascular disease [15][11].

In looksmaxxing communities, semaglutide is discussed as a systemic fat-loss tool, often under the heading of "leanmaxxing", whose effects on the face follow overall fat loss; the drug has no known mechanism for targeting facial fat specifically [22][24]. The phrase "Ozempic face" describes the gaunt or hollowed facial appearance that some people report after large, rapid weight loss on GLP-1 drugs [17]. Documented adverse effects are mainly gastrointestinal, and the US label carries a boxed warning about thyroid C-cell tumors seen in rodents [16].

Semaglutide has also become a cultural and commercial phenomenon. It was the top-selling drug in the United States in 2023, it was in shortage between 2022 and 2024, and a large market of compounded, counterfeit and "research-labelled" products grew around it, which the FDA and other regulators have repeatedly warned about [1][32].
infobox: Novo Nordisk (team including Jesper Lau, Thomas Kruse and Lotte Bjerre Knudsen's group) [1][31]

paras: Semaglutide is indicated in the United States to improve glycemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes and to reduce major adverse cardiovascular events in adults with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk [16][1]. Under the brand name Wegovy it is indicated for long-term weight reduction in people aged twelve and over with obesity, and in adults with overweight and at least one weight-related condition, and to reduce cardiovascular events in adults with established cardiovascular disease who are overweight or obese [1]. Wikipedia also lists use in metabolic-associated steatohepatitis under Wegovy and Kayshild [1].
Semaglutide is on the World Health Organization's List of Essential Medicines, and in 2024 it was among the most commonly prescribed medicines in the United States [1].

Appearance-focused users take semaglutide to lose body fat through reduced appetite. The weight loss is systemic rather than targeted, so any change to the face results from overall fat reduction [2][17]. Some people use prescription products; others, according to forum posts, use compounded or research-labelled supply obtained outside conventional prescribing [26][22]. Trials of the drug enrolled people with overweight or obesity (typically a BMI of 27 or 30 and above) or with type 2 diabetes, and no published trial has tested it in lean people seeking cosmetic leanness [14][4].

In the STEP program, once-weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg was tested as an adjunct to lifestyle intervention. STEP 1 enrolled 1,961 adults with obesity or overweight and no diabetes [14]. A 2022 meta-analysis of four randomized trials (3,613 people without diabetes) found a mean weight reduction of 11.85 percent favoring semaglutide over control [4], and a 2024 meta-analysis of four trials of at least 68 weeks (3,087 people) reported a weighted mean difference of about -12.1 percent relative to placebo [5]. In people with type 2 diabetes, STEP 2 compared 2.4 mg with 1.0 mg and placebo and examined weight outcomes in that group [9]. The two-year STEP 5 trial reported effects over a longer period [13].

Comparative trials place semaglutide below tirzepatide for weight loss. In a 2025 open-label phase 3b trial in adults with obesity without diabetes, the maximum tolerated dose of tirzepatide was compared directly with the maximum tolerated dose of semaglutide [3]. In the STEP 8 trial semaglutide 2.4 mg weekly was compared with daily liraglutide 3.0 mg [12].

Body composition has been studied in meta-analyses. A 2025 network meta-analysis of 22 randomized trials (2,258 participants) found that GLP-1 receptor agonists reduced total body weight, fat mass and lean mass, with lean-mass loss accounting for roughly a quarter of total weight loss; relative lean mass, as a percentage of body mass, was not significantly changed [6]. Wikipedia summarizes a 2024 review in which lean mass fell by 0 to 40 percent in individual studies while the ratio of lean to total mass rose [1].

Maintenance has also been examined. In STEP 4, participants who continued semaglutide after a run-in period were compared with those switched to placebo [10]. A 2025 meta-analysis of eight randomized trials in people with a BMI of at least 27 examined weight after GLP-1 drugs were stopped [7], and Wikipedia, citing a 2025 systematic review, states that people regain on average about two-thirds of lost weight within a year of stopping [1].

Wikipedia reports that the extension of STEP 1 found about two-thirds of the lost weight was regained one year after stopping treatment, with about one-third of the original loss (5.6 of 17.3 percentage points) kept after two years; the extension was reported in March 2023 [1]. Wikipedia also summarizes a 2025 SELECT post hoc analysis in adults aged 65 and over without diabetes that linked 104 weeks of semaglutide with a 26 percent lower predicted five-year dementia risk versus placebo [1].

The most common adverse effects are nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain and constipation. They are dose-dependent, usually mild to moderate, and tend to peak during dose escalation before easing [1]. A meta-analysis of semaglutide trials in people without diabetes found gastrointestinal adverse events were about 1.6 times as likely as on control [4]. Delayed gastric emptying can cause indigestion and, rarely, gastroparesis or bowel obstruction; gallstone and other biliary disease is also associated with treatment [1].

The US label carries a boxed warning for thyroid C-cell tumors, based on rodent studies, and the drug is contraindicated in people with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 [16]. The label also lists acute pancreatitis, diabetic retinopathy complications, hypoglycemia when combined with insulin or insulin secretagogues, acute kidney injury from volume depletion, and severe gastrointestinal reactions [16]. Wikipedia notes that cardiovascular outcome trials have not shown a statistically significant increase in pancreatitis or pancreatic cancer and that early retinopathy worsening has been attributed to rapid glucose lowering [1]. A meta-analysis of 21 trials of GLP-1 receptor agonists (99,599 patients) assessed mortality, cardiovascular events and serious adverse events [8].

The label says data in pregnancy are insufficient to evaluate risk and that animal studies suggest potential fetal risk [16]. Wikipedia reports that in January 2026 the FDA asked for removal of suicidal behavior and ideation warnings from GLP-1 receptor agonist labels [1].

Eye and mental-health questions have been reviewed by regulators. In June 2025 the EMA recommended listing non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) as a very rare side effect of semaglutide medicines, and Wikipedia reports that on 9 November 2026 the FDA ordered a NAION warning on all GLP-1 receptor agonist labels, citing a review of 126 randomized trials with a rate of 6.4 per 100,000 patients on the drugs versus 3.8 per 100,000 in comparison groups [1]. Iceland's medicines agency reported cases of suicidal thoughts and self-injury in July 2023, a preliminary FDA review in January 2024 found no evidence that the drug causes suicidal thoughts or actions, and in January 2026 the FDA asked for the suicidal-ideation warnings to be removed from GLP-1 labels [1].

The "Ozempic face" label has been used for facial hollowing, volume loss and skin laxity after fast, substantial weight loss. A 2024 dermatology article addresses whether the phenomenon reflects weight loss itself or the drug [17]. Men on semaglutide forums discuss facial fat loss as an expected consequence of leaning out [22].

Appearance researchers distinguish facial change that follows ordinary weight loss from change attributed to the drug itself; the 2024 dermatology article frames "Ozempic face" as a social-media term for the first, and no published trial has measured facial volume as an outcome of semaglutide treatment [17]. Members of looksmax.org have debated the topic, including a thread titled to predict that faces would "melt" because of Ozempic, while others on forums treat facial leanness as the goal [25][33].

Semaglutide is a GLP-1 analogue with about 94 percent sequence homology to the human hormone. It binds and activates GLP-1 receptors, reducing appetite and increasing satiety through brain pathways, slowing gastric emptying, and enhancing glucose-dependent insulin secretion while suppressing glucagon [16][1]. Weight loss is attributed mainly to reduced energy intake [1].

Compared with human GLP-1, semaglutide lacks the first six amino acids and has substitutions at two positions, including 2-aminoisobutyric acid, which blocks breakdown by dipeptidyl peptidase-4. A fatty-diacid chain attached to a lysine promotes albumin binding, which extends the half-life to about seven days and supports weekly injection [1][16].

Work on GLP-1 began in the 1970s, when Jens Juul Holst and Joel Habener started studying the hormone; by 1988 their work had revealed its marked metabolic effects, and in 2020 they shared the Warren Alpert Foundation Prize with Daniel J. Drucker [1]. In 1993 Michael Nauck infused GLP-1 into people with type 2 diabetes and found that it stimulated insulin and lowered blood glucose, but its very short action and side effects made it impractical as a treatment, which prompted a search for longer-acting analogues [1].

A parallel line of research began with Gila monster venom. In the 1980s Jean-Pierre Raufman and John Pisano at the NIH studied venom molecules, and in 1992 John Eng isolated exendin-4, which lowered blood glucose like GLP-1 but persisted far longer in the body [30]. A synthetic version, exenatide, was developed by Amylin Pharmaceuticals, later with Eli Lilly, and was approved by the FDA in 2005, showing that the GLP-1 receptor was a workable drug target [30]. Novo Nordisk's liraglutide, developed by a team led by Lotte Bjerre Knudsen, followed: it was approved for diabetes in 2010 and for weight management in 2014 [1][30][31].

A Novo Nordisk team including Jesper Lau, Thomas Kruse and Paw Bloch developed semaglutide as a once-weekly successor to liraglutide, with Knudsen overseeing the programme [1][31]. A 2015 paper by Lau and colleagues described its discovery as a once-weekly GLP-1 analogue [1]. A phase II trial of the once-weekly diabetes therapy began in June 2008, and the brand name Ozempic was attached to it [1]. Novo filed its US application in December 2016, an FDA advisory committee voted unanimously in favour in October 2017, and Ozempic was approved in December 2017, followed by Canada (January 2018), the EU (February 2018) and Japan (March 2018) [1].

An oral formulation, Rybelsus, was approved in the US in September 2019 and in the EU in April 2020 [1]. The higher-dose injectable for weight management, Wegovy, was approved in the US in June 2021 and in the EU in January 2022, after the STEP programme reported mean weight changes of about -14.9 percent at week 68 with semaglutide versus -2.4 percent with placebo in adults with obesity [1][14]. In March 2024 the FDA added an indication for reducing cardiovascular death, heart attack and stroke in adults with cardiovascular disease who have obesity or overweight, based on the SELECT trial of 17,604 participants [1][11]. Later approvals reported on Wikipedia include a liver-disease (MASH) indication for Wegovy in August 2025 and an oral semaglutide for weight management under the Wegovy name in December 2025 [1].

Semaglutide is prescription-only in the United States and elsewhere, sold by Novo Nordisk under the Ozempic, Wegovy and Rybelsus names, and as a generic by several companies in the Indian and Canadian markets [1]. Biosimilar-style products are the subject of registered comparison trials, for example a phase 3 study comparing a semaglutide injection with Wegovy for weight loss [29].

Semaglutide appears across fitness and appearance forums. T Nation members mention it in training logs alongside testosterone replacement and other peptides, and a clinic-affiliated poster tagged semaglutide among hormone-therapy services [26][27][28]. On looksmax.org, threads on appetite control and on a "leanmaxxing" face fat protocol discuss drugs as part of lean-face strategies [23][24]. Anthropological work cited on Wikipedia describes patients and clinicians adjusting dose, timing and access in practice, complicating the public view of the drug as an easy option [1].

Community posts cover several themes. Members report side effects such as nausea and motion-sickness-like symptoms in the first weeks [34]; one thread asks members to choose between semaglutide and amphetamine for appetite control while cutting, with replies discouraging amphetamine because of withdrawal [35]; another thread claims semaglutide slows ageing, which a reply questioned by asking whether the effect simply reflects eating less [36]. A separate thread asks whether sports and fitness culture among Gen Z has been undermined by Ozempic [37]. Posts on r/MenOnSema describe men tracking facial fat loss as they lose weight [22]. Forum members also pair the drug with resistance training and protein intake as a way of preserving muscle, a theme that mirrors the lean-mass findings in the body-composition literature [25][6].

Wikipedia notes that semaglutide is often framed publicly as an "easy way out" for weight loss, whereas an anthropological study of three Danish general practices found that patients and clinicians frequently adjusted dose, timing and administration to manage side effects, cost and access [1]. An ethnographic study of WeightWatchers members found that some people chose not to use these drugs, citing preferences for self-discipline and socially supported approaches; the author described this as "agentic disengagement" [1]. Wikipedia's article on GLP-1 receptor agonists reports that influencers and celebrities popularised the drugs for weight loss in the early 2020s [30].

The FDA declared a shortage of Ozempic and Wegovy in August 2022, and shortages in 2023 were worldwide, with new UK prescriptions paused for a period; in April 2024 Novo said it was running production around the clock and had budgeted US$6 billion for facility expansion that year [1]. While the drugs were on the FDA shortage list, US compounding pharmacies were allowed to prepare versions of semaglutide, and telehealth companies and online sellers marketed them directly to consumers [1]. In January 2026 Novo's chief executive cited up to 1.5 million US users of compounded GLP-1 drugs [1].

The FDA states that compounded and other unapproved GLP-1 products are not reviewed for safety, effectiveness and quality before they reach the market, and that compounding is intended for cases where an approved drug cannot meet a patient's needs [32]. The agency reports adverse events, some requiring hospitalization, linked to dosing errors with compounded injectable semaglutide, arising from patient self-measurement and in some cases provider miscalculation [32]. As of 31 May 2026 it had received 990 adverse event reports for compounded semaglutide, and it notes such counts are likely under-reported and do not always establish causation [32]. It has also warned about semaglutide sodium and semaglutide acetate, which it describes as different active ingredients from those in approved drugs, and about products sold online as "for research purposes" or "not for human consumption" that were marketed for human use [32].

Counterfeits have been documented: the EMA warned of falsified Ozempic pens in the EU on 18 October 2023, several people were hospitalized in Austria that month after using a suspected fake product, the UK's MHRA issued a warning on 23 November 2023, and the FDA warned US consumers on 21 December 2023 about counterfeit Ozempic in the supply chain [1][32]. Wikipedia reports that the counterfeit pens possibly contained insulin and led to hypoglycemia and seizures [1]. Forum posts describing peptide vials obtained outside conventional prescribing belong to the same gray market [26].

Semaglutide had the highest US drug sales in 2023, at US$38.6 billion, and by 2023 Novo Nordisk was the most valuable company in the EU, worth over US$500 billion, with its earnings contributing to Danish economic growth [1]. Wikipedia reports a 2022 US list price for Wegovy of US$1,349.02 a month and 2023 one-month list prices ranging from US$936 in the US to US$83 in France [1]. In November 2025 an agreement between the Trump administration and Novo set monthly prices of about US$245 for injectables for Medicare and Medicaid patients and users of the TrumpRx programme, and in February 2026 Novo announced that US list prices for Wegovy, Ozempic and Rybelsus would fall to US$675 per month from January 2027 [1].

Patent protection has begun to lapse outside the US. Wikipedia reports that the Indian patent expired in March 2026, after which dozens of brands launched, that Canadian data exclusivity ended in January 2026 with generic approvals from April 2026, and that the Brazilian patent expired in March 2026; US, European and Japanese expiry is expected around 2031 [1].

Beyond weight and diabetes, trials and analyses have examined semaglutide in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, chronic kidney disease, steatohepatitis and cardiovascular prevention [19][20][18][11]. Wikipedia lists observational and post hoc findings on knee osteoarthritis, dementia risk, macular degeneration and appetite-related behaviours as active areas of study, and reports a 2026 mouse study linking AgRP neurons in the hypothalamus to the drug's weight-lowering effect [1]. A phase 3 trial is comparing a semaglutide injection with Wegovy [29].

Semaglutide has been studied in many randomized trials. For weight management, STEP 1 (obesity without diabetes), STEP 2 (with type 2 diabetes), STEP 4 (maintenance), STEP 5 (two years) and STEP 8 (versus liraglutide) are the principal publications [14][9][10][13][12]. The SELECT trial tested semaglutide in people with obesity and established cardiovascular disease but no diabetes [11], and SUSTAIN-6 tested it in type 2 diabetes with cardiovascular risk [15]. Other randomized trials have examined heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and obesity [19], chronic kidney disease in type 2 diabetes [20] and nonalcoholic steatohepatitis [18]. A phase 3b trial compared tirzepatide with semaglutide [3], and a network meta-analysis compared them in type 2 diabetes [21]. No published trial has tested semaglutide specifically for facial appearance.

timeline.event: John Eng isolates exendin-4 from Gila monster venom, the basis of exenatide [30].
Exenatide becomes the first approved GLP-1 receptor agonist [30].
A phase II trial begins for a once-weekly Novo Nordisk GLP-1 therapy later named Ozempic [1].
SUSTAIN-6 reports cardiovascular outcomes of semaglutide in type 2 diabetes [15].
First US approval (Ozempic) for type 2 diabetes in December [1].
Oral semaglutide (Rybelsus) approved in the US in September [1].
STEP 1 reports weight outcomes in adults with obesity [14]; the FDA approves Wegovy for weight management in June [1].
FDA declares a shortage of Ozempic and Wegovy in August [1].
SELECT reports cardiovascular outcomes in obesity without diabetes [11]; regulators warn of counterfeit Ozempic pens in October to December [1].
FDA adds a cardiovascular-risk-reduction indication for Wegovy in March [1].

Head-to-head trial of tirzepatide versus semaglutide is published [3]; EMA recommends listing NAION as a very rare side effect in June, and an oral semaglutide is approved for weight management in December [1].
Generic semaglutide launches in India and approvals begin in Canada and Brazil [1].

lore.intro: Semaglutide is the most widely discussed GLP-1 drug in fitness and appearance circles, framed mainly as a way to reduce appetite and lean the body and face, with ongoing debate over facial volume loss, muscle retention, sourcing and rebound after stopping [22][23][25].

claims.claim: Semaglutide leans the face as total body fat falls.
claims.believers: Men posting on r/MenOnSema describe visible facial fat loss as their weight drops, and looksmax.org threads treat leanness as a route to sharper facial definition [22][24].
claims.experts: The drug is not known to act on facial fat selectively; trials measured total body weight and body composition, not facial change [6][17].

claims.claim: Rapid loss can produce "Ozempic face", a hollowed or aged look.
claims.believers: Users and commentators describe gauntness and sagging after fast loss, and some treat it as a cost to manage [22].
claims.experts: A 2024 dermatology review discusses the phenomenon as a social-media term and examines whether it differs from ordinary weight-loss-related facial change [17].

claims.claim: Most weight lost on GLP-1 drugs is muscle unless you resistance-train.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster states that most of the loss is muscle when no resistance training is done [25].
claims.experts: A 2025 network meta-analysis found lean mass made up about a quarter of total weight lost and that relative lean mass was unchanged for GLP-1 receptor agonists as a group; resistance training was not tested in that analysis [6].

claims.claim: Semaglutide combines well with testosterone therapy and other peptides for physique goals.
claims.believers: Forum logs list semaglutide beside testosterone, BPC-157 and supplements, and a clinic poster bundles it with hormone therapy [26][27].
claims.experts: No published trial has tested such combinations for physique or appearance; label warnings describe the drug alone [16].

claims.claim: Gray-market or compounded semaglutide is an equivalent substitute for the branded drug.
claims.believers: Posters describe sourcing peptide vials and tracking their own results [26].
claims.experts: The trials and the label concern the manufacturer's prescription products; no published trial has tested compounded or research-labelled supplies [16][14].

claims.claim: Weight stays off after stopping once the habit is built.
claims.believers: Some users present short courses as a reset for appetite and eating habits [23].
claims.experts: A 2025 meta-analysis and a Wikipedia-cited review report substantial regain after discontinuation, averaging about two-thirds within a year [7][1].

claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread presents semaglutide as an anti-ageing drug and pairs it with other compounds in a "lifefuel" stack [36].
claims.experts: The trials cited in this article tested weight, cardiovascular, kidney, liver and heart-failure outcomes rather than ageing as an endpoint [11][18][19][20]; a reply in the same thread asks whether any benefit is separate from eating less [36].

claims.claim: Semaglutide is a cleaner appetite suppressant than amphetamine for cutting.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster asks whether semaglutide or amphetamine is better for appetite control during a cut, having heard semaglutide "kills appetite" and is better long term [35].
claims.experts: The label describes semaglutide's effects on appetite and gastric emptying and lists gastrointestinal and other adverse effects [16]; no trial cited here compared it with amphetamine for appearance goals.

claims.claim: Early nausea and motion-sickness-like symptoms are normal and fade.
claims.believers: Users on looksmax.org report vomiting and new car sickness early on [34].
claims.experts: The label and Wikipedia describe nausea, vomiting and diarrhea as the most common effects, dose-dependent and tending to peak during dose escalation before easing [1][16].

claims.claim: Ozempic is making fitness culture and gym effort obsolete.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread asks whether sports and fitness culture among Gen Z is dying because of Ozempic [37].
claims.experts: The STEP trials tested semaglutide alongside lifestyle intervention, and a network meta-analysis reported that lean mass accounts for about a quarter of weight lost on GLP-1 drugs [14][6].

angle.text: Semaglutide lowers appetite so people eat less and lose body fat. Appearance-focused users take it to get lean, and the face typically slims along with the rest of the body; it does not remove fat from the face selectively.
